lessons.au: R.K. Narayan (poem: Ruskin Bond – ‘Grandma Climbs a Tree’)
lessons.words: sneer – speak in a very unkind way; frightful – unpleasant; face to face with – close to something and looking at it; reading it through – reading from beginning to end; crossly – a little angrily; mere skeleton – very thin; scowl – an angry look; tenacity – determination; cut in – interrupted at once; proposition – suggestion; mumble – say something not clearly; gloomily – in a way that things will not improve; sternly – seriously and strictly; tiptoed – walked quietly on toes; gesticulations – movements with hands and arms; snore – breathe noisily; apparition – ghost; scorpions – small poisonous creatures; slunk – moved quietly and secretly; laughing stock – object of ridicule; chum – a good friend; encased – covered closely; racked – made to suffer great pain; mortal weapon – deadly weapon; clutched – held tightly; burglar – a person who enters a building to steal; notorious – evil-minded; in a trice – very quickly; outcome – what actually happened; hold one’s peace – keep quiet; undaunted – without hesitation; chore – task; sherry – yellow or brown wine; upholding – making clear to the world
lessons.notes: Second form – seventh standard during British times. Poem ‘Grandma Climbs a Tree’ is part of this unit.
ab: Before you read
Can you guess why ‘I’ smiled? At his ignorance / forgetfulness in general / ready wit? [Choose the most appropriate one]
Ready wit. The boy cleverly added ‘forget’ as the fifth feature, which made the father smile.
Check your understanding (Paragraphs 1–5)
1. Swami’s father drew his attention to a report in the newspaper. What was the report about?

It was about a village lad who, while returning home by a jungle path, came face to face with a tiger. He fought the tiger and then stayed up a tree for half a day until people came and killed the tiger.

2. The report said that the boy stayed on the tree for half-a-day. Why did he do so? a. He wanted to watch the tiger from the top of a tree. b. He wanted someone to kill the tiger. c. He wanted to take rest for some time.
b. He wanted someone to kill the tiger. (He waited in the tree until people came and killed it.)
3. Swami said that a very strong and grown-up person might have fought with the tiger. Do you think he made this remark out of his (a) experience (b) wisdom (c) belief?
c. belief. Swami believed that strength and age make a person brave enough to fight a tiger.
4a. ‘Can you prove you have courage?’ Swami’s father said. Was he joking? Or, serious?
He was serious.
4b. Was it a challenge? Or, a command?
At first it was a challenge (‘Can you prove you have courage?’). It soon became a command: ‘You must sleep alone hereafter.’
5. The place where Swami usually slept was ……………………. (Fill in the blank)
in the passage, beside his granny.
6. What is disgraceful, according to Swami’s father?
It is disgraceful for Swami to sleep beside his granny or mother like a baby.
Check your understanding (Paragraphs 6–9)
1. What do you think was the practice of granny before she went to bed?
Granny used to tell Swami a story before he went to sleep.
2. Was Swami really sleeping? Or, was he pretending?
He was pretending. He made signs to silence his granny and snored under the blanket to avoid talking and to escape from his father.
3. To Swami, his father looked like an ………………… (Fill in the blank)
apparition (ghost).
4. Why do you think Swami looked at his granny and his mother while following his father to the room?
He was pleading silently for help. He hoped one of them would stop his father from making him sleep alone in the office room.
5a. ‘There might be scorpions behind your law books,’ said Swami. Had he seen them earlier? Or, were there scorpions really?
He had not seen them. There were no scorpions; he was making an excuse.
5b. Was it a trick to escape from his father?
Yes. It was a trick to escape from sleeping alone in the office room.
Check your understanding (Paragraphs 10–13)
1. Swami wished that the tiger hadn’t spared the boy, which means… a. he didn’t want the boy to be alive. b. he didn’t want the tiger to be alive.
a. he didn’t want the boy to be alive.
2. As silence deepened in the room, what was Swami reminded of?
He was reminded of the stories of devils and ghosts he had heard in his life.
3. Which place in the room did Swami think was safe, compact and reassuring?
The space under the bench.
4. Swami touched ……………………………………..in the room instead of granny. (Fill in the blank appropriately)
the wooden leg of the bench.
5. Swami saw a moving creature in the room. It was ………………… a. his shadow b. a scorpion c. a man
c. a man. It was the burglar hiding under the bench, though Swami thought it was a devil.
Check your understanding (Paragraphs 14–17)
1. Who cried, ‘Aiyo! Something has bitten me’?
The burglar cried out.
2. Who did father, cook and a servant stumble upon?
The burglar lying amidst the furniture with a bleeding ankle.
3. Why were congratulations showered on Swami?
Because he had bitten one of the most notorious house-breakers of the district, and the police were grateful to him.
4. Do you think Swami really wanted to join the police? If not, what did he want to be?
No. He wanted to be an engine driver, a railway guard or a bus conductor.
5. Did Swami muster up courage to sleep alone after the burglar incident?
No. He went back to sleeping beside his granny in his usual place.
6. Who supported Swami – his mother or his granny?
His mother supported him. She said, ‘You let him sleep where he likes.’
Think about the text
1. A report about a boy in the newspaper was an unexpected event in Swami’s life. Justify.
The report led his father to challenge Swami to sleep alone in the office room. This changed Swami’s peaceful routine and forced him to face his fear of darkness.
2. Swami made a comment on the newspaper report. Was he right? How did his view differ from that of his father?

Swami felt that strength and age matter. His father felt that courage matters more than strength or age. Swami was partly right that strength helps, but his father was right that courage is essential. Accept reasoned answers.
3. What desperate attempts did Swami make to escape from his father?
He offered to sleep in the hall, claimed there were scorpions, asked for a lamp, asked the door to be left open, pleaded with his mother and granny, and pretended to be asleep.
4. Why did Swami conclude that his father’s proposition was frightful?
Sleeping alone in the dark office room, away from his granny, was frightening for him.
5. As the night advanced, Swami felt that something terrible would happen to him. What would it be? How would it happen?
He feared that devils or ghosts would come and carry him away. He thought the devil would come up, pull him out and tear him.
6. There was absolute silence in the room. In spite of it, some noises reached Swami’s ears. What were they?
The ticking of the clock, the rustle of trees, snoring sounds and night insects humming.
7. Narrate Swami’s dreadful experience when he was lying under the bench.

He had a nightmare in which a tiger chased him and his feet stuck to the ground. He woke up in fear, felt lonely and saw something moving. He believed a devil was coming to tear him, so he crawled out, hugged it and bit it with his teeth.
8. How was Swami honoured by his classmates, teacher and the headmaster?
His classmates looked at him with respect, his teacher patted his back, and the headmaster said he was a true scout.
9. Why did father want Swami to sleep alone in the office room?
He wanted Swami to overcome his fear of darkness, to learn to be brave and to cultivate good habits.
10. Who do you think was wiser, Swami or his father? Justify your preference.
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Sample: The father was wiser, as he tried to build courage and self-reliance in his son instead of letting him depend on his granny.
11. Why did Swami feel relieved at the end?
Because his father gave up the plan and let him sleep where he liked, so he could sleep beside his granny again.
12. Suppose you are Swami of the story. Write a brief letter to your friend describing how you helped to catch a burglar in your house.

ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Sample letter: Dear Ravi, I hope you are well. Last night a burglar entered our house. While he was hiding under the bench in my father’s office room, I bit his ankle. He cried out and my father, the cook and the servant caught him. The police were pleased and the headmaster praised me. Yours affectionately, Swami.
13. Put the words (caring, protective, innocent, tricky, authoritative, disciplined, helpless, nervous) in the appropriate columns: Swami’s father / Mother / Granny / Swami.
Swami’s father: authoritative, disciplined. Mother: protective. Granny: caring, innocent. Swami: tricky, nervous, helpless. (Accept reasoned placements.)
Enrich your vocabulary – Task 1 (Homophones)
1. We had _____ many apples to carry. (too/two)
too
2. I _____ a horse at the Marina Beach. (road/rode)
rode
3. Did you have a _____ for lunch? (pear/pair)
pear
4. The books are over _____ on the shelf. (their/there)

Enrich your vocabulary – Task 2 (Fill in the blanks)

This is a __________ (storey/story) told by a __________ (night/knight). Once he received a letter. When he __________ (red/read) it __________ (through/threw), he could not believe his own eyes. __________ (Far/For), it was written __________ (buy/by) none other than the queen of the land. She asked him to meet her __________ (at/yet) a secret place. The knight was in a fix. But he thought __________ (of/off) a plan to tide over this problem. He __________ (vent/went) to the meeting place, not alone, but along with his __________ (fair/fare) wife. Can you guess what happened then?

story; knight; read; through; For; by; at; of; went; fair. (Complete: This is a story told by a knight. Once he received a letter. When he read it through, he could not believe his own eyes. For it was written by none other than the queen of the land. She asked him to meet her at a secret place. The knight was in a fix. But he thought of a plan to tide over this problem. He went to the meeting place, not alone, but along with his fair wife.)
Enrich your vocabulary – Task 3 (Unscramble the words)
1. a t r t e f l (praise)
flatter
2. b o u d t (suspect)
doubt
3. r a g t e d y (unhappy ending)
tragedy
4. r a g f e n m t (a piece)
fragment
5. r a e t l (careful)
alert
6. c a c s r i y t (short supply)
scarcity
7. y m t s a t h p e i c (not cruel)
sympathetic
Listen and comprehend (Listening script – Unit 1)
1. Why do you think the audience, on hearing the dialogue, burst into laughter?
The actor mixed up the words, saying ‘stars were barking, dogs were twinkling’ and ‘the thief broke the clock and took away the wall’, which was ridiculous and funny.
2. Try to repeat the words as delivered by the actor.
‘Stars were barking, dogs were twinkling, and the thief broke the clock and took away the wall.’ (Accept the learner’s attempt.)
3. If you had been the actor, how would you have said it?
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Sample: ‘Stars were twinkling, dogs were barking, and a thief broke the wall and took away the clock.’
Speak well – Language function: Refusing invitation
Imagine that Swami receives advice from his father and granny. How would Swami say that he accepts or refuses it? Write a dialogue using the expressions given.

ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Sample dialogue – Father: ‘Swami, you should sleep alone in the office room.’ Swami: ‘That’s a very good idea, Father. Thank you.’ (accepting). Granny: ‘Would you like to hear a story tonight?’ Swami: ‘Thank you for the offer, Granny. I think, on the whole, I’d rather not. Thank you all the same.’ (refusing)
Read and respond
Task 1: Mr. Khanna was surprised at the astrologer’s prediction. What made him feel so?
The astrologer knew details of his family, such as his children, his shopping and his ration card, which made Khanna feel impressed.
Task 1: Why wasn’t the astrologer able to predict Mr. Khanna’s future?
The astrologer only knew facts about the past and present which he had gathered, and he could not truly predict the future.
Task 1: In the conversation, who do you think has better common sense?
Accept reasoned answers. Mr. Khanna, as he realised that the astrologer’s knowledge was based on ordinary facts.
Task 2: Which word in the passage gives the opposite meaning of what was meant to be said?
‘hardly’ – it should have been ‘hard’. ‘Worked hardly’ means barely worked, which is the opposite of the intended meaning.
Task 3: Look at the cartoon. Interpret it orally with your partner. What is funny as shown in the cartoon?
ಚಿತ್ರದಲ್ಲಿ ಒಂದು ಲಿಫ್ಟ್ (lift) ಒಳಗೆ ಜನರು ನಿಂತಿರುವ ದೃಶ್ಯವಿದೆ. ಹಾಸ್ಯ ಇರುವುದು ಲಿಫ್ಟ್‌ನಲ್ಲಿರುವ ವ್ಯಕ್ತಿಗಳ ಭಂಗಿ ಮತ್ತು ಸನ್ನಿವೇಶದಲ್ಲಿ. ನಿಖರ ಹಾಸ್ಯ ವಿವರ (ಪರಿಶೀಲಿಸಿ – ಚಿತ್ರ ಸ್ಪಷ್ಟವಿಲ್ಲ; ಮಕ್ಕಳೊಂದಿಗೆ ಚರ್ಚಿಸಿ).

Learn grammar through communication – Use of Modals
1. Please return my library books. (Begin with ‘will’) Function: Requesting
Will you return my library books? (Requesting)
2. The files are heavy. I’ll carry them for you. (Begin with ‘would’) Function: Offering help
Would you like me to carry the files for you? (Offering help)
3. That’s your essay. Perhaps you will have no objection if I see it. (Begin with ‘May’) Function: Seeking permission
May I see your essay? (Seeking permission)
4. Let me switch on the fan, OK? (Begin with ‘Do you’) Function: Offering help
Do you want me to switch on the fan? (Offering help)
5. ‘Bring the books to my office.’ (Begin with ‘would’) Function: Requesting politely
Would you bring the books to my office? (Requesting politely)
Make reference – Dictionary
Task 1: Based on the entries of ‘lorry’ and ‘truck’, what do the entries tell us?

a. lorry is a word used in British English. b. In British English truck means an open railway vehicle, not a motor vehicle. c. In American English truck means a motor vehicle, the same as lorry. d. truck can also mean a simple hand-pulled or hand-pushed cart in both British and American English.
Task 2: What does ‘derog’ mean in the entry for ‘windbag’?
‘derog’ means derogatory. The word windbag is insulting, so a person may feel offended if called a windbag.
Task 3: With the help of a dictionary, find out what you can understand about: 1. cheque and check as nouns. 2. hire and rent as verbs.

Cheque: a written order to a bank to pay money. Check (noun): examination or verification; in American English, the bill in a restaurant. Hire (verb): pay to use something temporarily or to employ someone. Rent (verb): pay to use something owned by another person.

POETRY – Before you read (Grandma Climbs a Tree)
a–c. Childish habits given: marbles, kites, bike riding. d–e. Add more.
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Sample: Playing hopscotch; eating candies; singing rhymes.
Understand the poem (Grandma Climbs a Tree)
1. The speaker does not call his grandmother ‘childish’. What else was she according to him? Why? (lines 1–4)
She was a genius, because she could climb trees, spreading or high, and was up their branches in a trice.
2. Identify the lines that suggest that grandma had been in the habit of climbing trees for a long period.
‘Ever since childhood, she’d had this gift’ (line 5) and ‘Having learned to climb from a loving brother when she was six’ (line 13).
3. Look at lines 7 and 8. Who do you think would tell her so?
Her family members, such as her children or relatives, would tell her that climbing should stop when one grew old.
4. Do you find anything odd in the reply given by the grandma? Why? (lines 10–11)
Yes. Instead of growing old gracefully she says she will ‘grow disgracefully’, which is an odd and playful reply.
5. Others had feared that granny would fall one day. Did this happen? Or did something else happen? (lines 15–18)
She did not fall, but while the family was in town she climbed a tree and could not come down. She had to be rescued.
6. What had the doctor recommended? What was the reaction of the kids?
The doctor recommended a quiet week in bed. The kids were relieved and tucked her up well.
7. Quote the lines which suggest how wholeheartedly granny enjoyed climbing a tree.
‘happier in a tree than in a lift’ (line 6) and ‘She’d be up their branches in a trice’ (line 2).
8. ‘My dad knew his duties.’ What did he think his duty was?
He thought it was his duty to fulfil his mother’s wish and build her a house in a treetop.
9. Look at the picture given below the title. Quote the lines that might have guided the artist to draw that.
(ಚಿತ್ರ ಆಧಾರಿತ) ‘Made her a tree-house with windows and a door’ and ‘She sits there in state and drinks sherry with me’ may have guided the artist.
Read and appreciate (Grandma Climbs a Tree)
A1. Does the behaviour of grandma strike you as unusual? Support your view quoting her ways and responses.
Yes. Way 1: Grandma climbing a tree at sixty-two. Response: ‘Well I’ll grow disgracefully, I can do it better.’ Response: She asked for a house in a treetop instead of staying in bed.
A2. Discuss whether what the grandma was doing was graceful or otherwise.
Accept reasoned answers. Her climbing was not graceful by usual standards, but it was graceful in spirit because it gave her joy and independence.
A3. Both the narrator and his father were considerate towards Grandma. Substantiate with textual support.
The narrator tucked her up well and the father said, ‘You’ll have what you want, dear. I’ll start work tonight.’ He built a tree-house with windows and a door.
A4. If you were to divide the poem into two parts, which line would you pick as the beginning of the second part? Why?
‘The outcome was different – while we were in town’ (line 17). From here the poem shifts from the climbing to the accident and its aftermath.
B1. Write at least 5 pairs of rhyming words.
gift – lift; town – down; stronger – longer; undaunted – wanted; tonight – right.
B2. ‘It was like a brief season’ – name the figure of speech. What are the two things compared?
Simile (‘like’). Her confinement to bed is compared to a season in hell, showing how painful it was for her.
B3. ‘For being happier in a tree than in a lift’. What is suggested through this line?
She loved nature and freedom more than comfort and convenience; she enjoyed the outdoors more than modern comforts.
B4. Rewrite without using ‘not’: ‘There was not a tree she hadn’t been up.’ Give examples of double negatives.
She had been up every tree in the garden. Double negatives examples: ‘It is not impossible that he will come.’ ‘She is not unkind.’ ‘I could not help but laugh.’
C. Draw pictures for: 1. An aged woman confined to bed. 2. Every breeze whispered of summer and dancing leaves. 3. Being happier in a tree than in a lift. 4. I will grow disgracefully.
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. (Personal drawing task.)

lessons.t: There’s a Girl by the Tracks!
lessons.au: Deven Kanal (poem: William Shakespeare – ‘Quality of Mercy’, for memorization)
lessons.words: suburban – of a place outside a city; commuter – one who travels to work daily; swarm – rush; hurtle – move fast; tenuous – weak or shaky; panic – suddenly feel frightened; clattering – making a loud sound; muffled – silenced; thud – low sound; gasp – deep breath taken when surprised; emanate – come from; impulsively – without thinking; frantically – with no hope; wary – worried; shove – push roughly; sprint – run very fast; sprawled – lie stretched; gash – deep cut; gingerly – nervously; implore – request; fiancé – man a woman is engaged to; lanky – tall and thin; treading water – making no progress; to grind out – say with effort; black out – become unconscious; hang around – wait; suture – stitch; barely speak – not able to speak; partly sedated – half awake due to drugs; strain’d – forced; droppeth – drops; blest – blessed; sceptre – decorated rod of a king; temporal – worldly; majesty – royal power; doth – does; dread – threat; enthroned – seated; attribute – quality; likest – like; seasons – tempers
lessons.notes: Mumbai local train incident, December 2010. Quality of Mercy is a memorization poem from Shakespeare’s ‘The Merchant of Venice’.
ab: Before you read
1. If you had been there at the place shown in the picture, how would you have reacted? (Begin with ‘I would have’)
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. (ಚಿತ್ರ ಆಧಾರಿತ – ಪಠ್ಯಪುಸ್ತಕದ ಚಿತ್ರ ನೋಡಿ) Sample: I would have immediately rushed to help the injured person and called for help.

Imagine you lent money to your friend who doesn’t return it when you need it. What would you do? (a. forgive b. punish c. ignore d. pity e. sympathize f. other)
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Sample: I would sympathize with him and gently remind him to return it when he can.
2. Which quality of Baleshwar strikes you as great?
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Sample: His courage and compassion in helping a stranger without any hesitation.
Check your understanding (Paragraphs 1–5)
1. ‘It’s a regular scene.’ What was regular about the scene? (para 1)
Commuters rush in and out of the packed suburban train at every halt, squeezing into crowded coaches.
2. Roma tried to settle into a corner near the door. Was she right in doing this? What would you have done?
Accept reasoned answers. She was not wise, as standing near an open door in a packed train is unsafe. Sample: I would have held a firm handrail and moved to a safer place inside the coach.
3. ‘There’s a girl by the tracks!’ the voices cried out. Whose voices do you think those were?
The voices of the passengers in Baleshwar’s train, who had seen the girl lying beside the tracks.
4. Baleshwar was impulsive in taking a decision because ……………………… (para 3)
he could not bear to see a young woman lying injured by the tracks and wanted to save her immediately.
5. The dictionary says ‘callous’ means ‘unconcerned’. In this situation, who were ‘callous’ towards the accident?
The passengers in Baleshwar’s compartment, who did not volunteer to help because they were afraid of getting involved.
6. Identify two more verbs or verbal phrases in paragraph 5 that describe Baleshwar’s movement.
‘jumped off’ and ‘sprint back’ (also ‘shoved himself’ is given).
Check your understanding (Paragraphs 6–9)
1. Where did Baleshwar find Roma at last?
He found her sprawled by the side of the tracks, between two stations about five kilometres apart in Thane district.
2. ‘Behenji, aap theek hai?’ But there was no response and no help in sight. Why was it so? (para 6)
Roma was unconscious and badly injured, and they were alone in an isolated place between two stations, with no one nearby to help.
3. Fill in the table with appropriate details.

Roma Talreja: Age 21; Education: B.Com graduate; State: Maharashtra (from Pune); Profession: call centre executive; Reason for boarding the train: going home after her shift. Baleshwar Mishra: Age 20; Education: high-school dropout; State: Uttar Pradesh (from Mirzapur); Profession: unemployed, looking for a job; Reason for boarding the train: going home after spending the day with a friend.
Check your understanding (Paragraphs 10–14)
1. Who volunteered to help Baleshwar?
The middle-aged tempo-truck driver who spoke Gujarati stopped and helped him.
2. ‘Roma stirred and her eyes fluttered open.’ What could have made her react so?
The jolt of the truck moving forward made her stir and open her eyes.
3. Fill in the columns about Dinesh (para 14).
Name: Dinesh Talreja; Job: marketing job at a retail outlet; Place: Ulhasnagar; Vehicle: motorcycle.
Check your understanding (Paragraphs 15–20)
1. ‘Oh, I couldn’t thank him,’ Baleshwar thought. Who do you think he couldn’t thank?
The truck driver, who had slipped away with his truck after helping.
2. Why did Baleshwar revisit the spot where Roma had fallen?
He wanted to look for Roma’s belongings, as Dinesh had said her cell phone and handbag were missing.
3. Baleshwar got some assurance from a railway employee. What was that?
The employee assured him that some of Roma’s belongings had been found.
4. Roma said, ‘I think it’s astonishing’. What was astonishing?
That a stranger would jump off a train and risk his life to save her.
Think about the text

1. Put the incidents relating to Roma in the right order: a. Roma lost her foothold. b. The train hurtled ahead. c. Roma was thrown out of the coach. d. Roma was jammed between two women. e. Roma panicked.
d, b, a, e, c
2. Set Baleshwar’s actions in the right sequence: a. crossed the track. b. carried the girl. c. saw the girl bleeding. d. requested motorists to help. e. prayed silently.
c, e, b, a, d
3. Write briefly the personal details (qualification and profession) of Roma Talreja and Baleshwar Mishra.

Understand the poem (Quality of Mercy)
1. Mercy is compared to something in the first two lines. What is it? How is this comparison apt? Justify.
Mercy is compared to the gentle rain from heaven. It is apt because mercy falls softly and quietly, and it refreshes and nourishes the one who receives it, just as rain nourishes the earth below.
2. The speaker says that mercy is twice blessed. What does she mean by this?
Mercy blesses both the one who gives it and the one who receives it.
3. ‘Sceptre shows the force of temporal power’. In contrast, what or whose quality does mercy stand for?
Mercy stands for the quality of compassion and kindness, which is a divine (God-like) attribute, above worldly power.
4. Classify the qualities into temporal power and divine attributes: love, revenge, sympathy, tyranny, cruelty, miserliness, mercy, hatred, tit-for-tat attitude, compassion.
Temporal power: revenge, tyranny, cruelty, miserliness, hatred, tit-for-tat attitude. Divine attributes: love, sympathy, mercy, compassion.
Read and appreciate (Quality of Mercy)
1. Read the first two lines. Explain the simile briefly.
Mercy is compared to gentle rain that falls from heaven on the earth below. As rain benefits everything beneath it, mercy benefits everyone.
2. How do you interpret the speaker’s view of mercy as twice blessed?
It blesses the giver, who gains the joy of helping, and the receiver, who is relieved of suffering.
3. The speaker says mercy is the mightiest of the mightiest. How does she justify this?
Mercy is enthroned in the heart of kings and is an attribute of God himself. It softens justice and makes earthly power show likeness to God’s power, which makes it mightier than the sceptre.
4. Can you think of any story where virtues like mercy, compassion or sacrifice are highlighted?

5. This poem has fourteen lines but it is not a sonnet. Justify.
Its rhyme scheme and line endings do not follow the strict pattern of a Shakespearean sonnet, so it is a poem of fourteen lines but not a sonnet in form.

b) How do trees stand?

Understand the poem – ‘I Am the Land’
1. Who do you think is the speaker of the poem?
The land (the earth) is the speaker.
2. ‘I wait’ in line 1 suggests the feeling of a) annoyance b) patience c) disgust.
b. patience.
3. In line 2 ‘you’ is repeated. Do you think it refers to the same person?
No. It refers to different people, such as the owners and users who claim and exploit the land.
4. Bring out the contrast between the reader and the speaker as suggested in lines 4, 5 and 6.
The reader (people) shout, buy and claim the land, while the speaker (land) lies patient and waits silently.
5. ‘muddy holes’ refers to a) virtual holes b) intention of the speaker c) commotion created by the reader.
c. commotion created by the reader.
6. What does the phrase ‘car lot eyes stare’ suggest? Draw the picture if you can.
(ಚಿತ್ರ ಆಧಾರಿತ – ಪಠ್ಯಪುಸ್ತಕದ ಚಿತ್ರ ನೋಡಿ) It suggests the land being used as a parking lot for cars and seen only for commercial gain. Learner to draw.
7. Classify the actions: chokes, shoots, waits, shouts, sings, rejoices, destroys, plants, dances, tramples, grows, says he owns, faces the challenge, kills.
The Land: waits, grows, faces the challenge. A common man/child: plants, dances, sings, rejoices. A war-mongerer: shoots, chokes, destroys, tramples, kills, shouts, says he owns.
8. Pick out the line that expresses the speaker’s self-assertion.
‘YOU CANNOT PUT A FENCE AROUND THE PLANET EARTH’.
Read and appreciate – ‘I Am the Land’
1. ‘I wait’ is repeated five times. What quality of the speaker is highlighted?
Patience and endurance, together with the land’s quiet strength.
2. Pick out figures of speech (personification).
‘A chainlink necklace chokes me now’; ‘I lie patient’; ‘tickles me, plants life’.
3. Pick out other images from the poem.
Soldiers with guns; children dancing; someone singing; fruit, grass and trees growing; muddy holes.
4. ‘YOU CANNOT PUT A FENCE AROUND THE PLANET EARTH’ – tone of weakness or self-assertion?
Self-assertion. The land declares that no one can own or confine the whole earth.
5. Which line do you enjoy reciting most? Give reasons.
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Learner’s own choice with reason.
Recite and enjoy – ‘I Draw Nourishment’
Is the theme of this poem the same as that of ‘I am the land, I wait’? Who does the word ‘I’ stand for in ‘I Draw Nourishment’?
Yes, both poems speak of nature’s patience and selfless giving. The ‘I’ stands for a tree, which feeds on dirt and slush, gives shade and fruit, and never does harm.

ab: Before you read
Discuss: How can a simple or common man contribute to strengthen the country?
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Sample: By doing honest work, paying taxes, keeping the surroundings clean, following laws and helping others.
What is the poet saying about India in the lines ‘Better than Heaven or Arcadia / I love thee O my India’?
The poet says India is more precious than heaven or an ideal place, and that he loves it deeply.
Check your understanding (Paragraphs 1–3)
1. Ambedkar spent most of his life in ………… a) purchasing books b) attending conferences c) reading books d) importing books
c. reading books.
2. Pick out the word in the first paragraph which means ‘a quality that makes a person or thing different from another’.
‘trait’ (Hint: it appears as a quality of Ambedkar’s character).
3. How did the fourteenth amendment of the American Constitution benefit the Black Americans?
It gave them freedom, which inspired Ambedkar to see a parallel for the Depressed Classes in India.
4. What did Mahatma Phule work for?
He worked for a classless society and for women’s uplift.
5. Mooknayak, Bahishkrit Bharat and Samata were ………… a) voice mails b) newspapers c) political parties
b. newspapers.
6. Gandhiji termed the depressed classes as ………………
Harijans.
Check your understanding (Paragraphs 4–6)
1. Draft is a banking term. How is the word used in the context of this lesson?
Here ‘draft’ means the proposed text of the Constitution, which the Assembly discussed and finalised.
2. Dr. Ambedkar was not in the Congress party. Yet he was made the chairman of the drafting committee. Why?
Because the farsighted and objective leadership of the Indian National Congress recognised his ability and requested him to serve on the committee.
3. He raised it ‘brick by brick’. In this context, what was raised?
The edifice of the Fundamental Rights and the other provisions of the Constitution.
4. Who were the other notable members of the drafting committee?
Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, K.M. Munshi and N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar.
5. Ambedkar had ‘rare gifts’. What were they? Can you think of your own gifts?
His gifts were tact, frankness, patience, and the ability to explain complicated legal concepts in simple language. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. (Own gifts – learner’s answer.)
6. Constitution is a fundamental document to both the ruler and the ruled. How?
It defines the powers of the State organs and limits their authority, protecting citizens from tyranny and oppression, and it defines the rights of citizens.
Check your understanding (Paragraphs 7–10)
1. Nehru chose Dr. Ambedkar as law minister for three reasons. What are they?
(a) His skill in law and legislation; (b) his vision of social justice; (c) his success in campaigns against social injustice.
2. Are you aware of the facilities provided by the Social Welfare Department? Mention any two.
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Sample: Scholarships for SC/ST students and hostel facilities.
3. After independence, members of the Scheduled Castes have found doors opened to them. How?
They are enrolling in institutes of higher learning, entering public services and occupying high offices of State, such as judges, ambassadors and governors.
4. All people should be given equal opportunities to prove themselves. How are members of the Scheduled Castes proving themselves?
They have acquitted themselves creditably as judges, ambassadors, governors and in other positions of responsibility.
5. Babasaheb Ambedkar considers public agitation in free India as unconstitutional. Why?

In a democracy based on free and fair elections, agitations such as civil disobedience and non-cooperation lead to loss of lives and public property; the right to rebellion applies only to governments without people’s consent.
6. Social discrimination still exists in India. Debate in the class.
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Learner’s own debate points.
Check your understanding (Paragraphs 11–14)
1. What were the opinions of the Buddha and Avvai regarding caste divisions?
The Buddha said the only valid divisions are between the noble/wholesome and the ignoble/unwholesome. Avvai said there are only two castes: the charitable (superior) and the misers (inferior).
2. Caste system in India is in a strong position because of ……………… (fill in from paragraph 11)
its power structure.
3. Why did the British magnify caste distinctions?
Under their policy of ‘Divide and Rule’, to divide the people of India further and strengthen their hegemony.
4. The word ‘hegemony’ means ……… a) distinction b) control c) strength
b. control.
5. ‘They brought about a veritable revolution in social thought.’ a) Who are ‘they’? b) What revolution? c) How?

a) Mahatma Gandhi and Dr. Ambedkar. b) A revolution in social thought that repudiated caste and proclaimed the oneness of the Hindu community. c) Gandhi reminded higher castes of their duty to the Depressed Classes; Ambedkar reminded them of the equal rights of these classes.
6. Why did Nehru describe Dr. Ambedkar as ‘a symbol of revolt’?
Because of his perseverance, persistence and opposition to injustice, which kept people awake to the issues and roused the groups that had suffered for so long.
Think about the text
1. Ambedkar had a great thirst for books when he was a student. Explain.
He was a voracious reader. He bought books by cutting his daily needs, bought about 2,000 old books in New York, and sent 32 boxes of books to India after the Second Round Table Conference.
2. How did the fourteenth amendment of the US Constitution and Mahatma Phule influence Ambedkar?

The fourteenth amendment gave freedom to Black Americans and made him see a parallel for the Depressed Classes. Phule’s life and work for a classless society and women’s uplift made him devote his life to the underprivileged.
3. There were great luminaries on the Drafting Committee. Dr. Ambedkar is remembered as its pilot. Give reasons.
He anticipated every need of the new polity, raised the Fundamental Rights, and explained the provisions with tact, patience and clarity in simple language.
4. Write a short note on Dr. Ambedkar’s idea of the three pillars of State.
He understood the mutuality of the legislature, executive and judiciary and believed the jurisdiction of each must be clear and untrammelled. He also gave importance to the role of citizens.
5. What are the significant observations of Dr. Ambedkar on the Constitution?
The Constitution is a fundamental document that defines the position and power of the three organs of the State and limits their authority to prevent tyranny and oppression.
6. What might have prompted Nehru to choose Dr. Ambedkar as the law minister?
His skill in law, his vision of social justice and his success in campaigns against social injustice.
7. What made Dr. Ambedkar describe civil disobedience, non-cooperation and satyagraha as the ‘grammar of anarchy’?
In a democracy such methods, when used against an elected government, invariably result in loss of lives and public property.
8. How did Dr. Ambedkar and Mahatma Gandhi try to wipe out caste discrimination?
Gandhi reminded the higher castes of their duties towards the Depressed Classes, while Ambedkar reminded them of the equal rights of these classes.

Before you read – ‘The Song of India’
What is the poet saying about India in the above lines? Discuss.
The poet says India is better than heaven or Arcadia; he loves it and will share that love with every nation.
Understand the poem – ‘The Song of India’
1. Identify the two speakers in the poem. What does the speaker want to sing about?
The two speakers are the poet and the Mother (India). The poet wants to sing about India’s beauty and glory, such as the Himalayas, the seas and the clear dawn.
2. What are epics? Why does the poet call the temples ‘epics in stone’?
Epics are long narrative poems of heroic deeds. The temples are called epics in stone because they carry the glorious history and stories of the nation in carved stone.
3. Who does the poet mean by ‘your children that died to call you their own’?
The freedom fighters and martyrs who sacrificed their lives for the country’s freedom.
4. According to the poet, what is the contribution of the seers and prophets?
They hewed the straight path for the pilgrims, showing humanity the right way spiritually and morally.
5. Why is the poet ‘querulous’? What does he want to do?
He is complaining because the Mother asks him to sing of the poverty and problems too. He wants to sing a pure, complete and perfect song of India.
6. How is he answered? Describe the vision. (stanza 4)

The Mother rises, draped in blue sky, with milk-white oceans around her, and writes the Book of the Morrow. Her forehead opens like the destiny of earth, the night flees and the sunbeam appears as a hand that saves.
7. What do the night, the sun god and the clear dawn represent?
The night represents ignorance and sorrow; the sun god represents enlightenment and hope; the clear dawn represents a bright new beginning for the nation.
Read and appreciate – ‘The Song of India’
1. What is the picture of India that you get in stanza 1?
A beautiful land with snow-capped Himalayas, three seas washing its coast, and a clear dawn with golden streaks.
2. How does the poet describe the Mother’s anger? Name the figure of speech used in stanza 2.
Her words beat into his ears like a gong and fly about him like great white birds. The figure of speech is simile.
3. Explain the lines ‘A song bathed in the stainless blue unvapouring in the void.’
The poet wants a pure, eternal song of India, which will never fade away or vanish into nothingness.
4. What does ‘the Motherland writing the Book of the Morrow’ signify?
It signifies that India itself will write its own bright future, shaped by its people and their hope.
5. Write in brief your vision of the future of India.

lessons.notes: Set in 1942 during the Quit India Movement. The students’ silent march and the cyclostyling machine used to print copies of Gandhiji’s speech are the key incidents.
ab: Answer the following questions
1. Why had the students been marching? How was it an unusual march?

The students marched to protest against British rule during the Quit India Movement. It was unusual because they marched in complete silence, with no slogans or shouts, even though the police were all around them.
2. A police officer was seen talking to the student leaders. Can you guess what the officer had been talking to them about?
The officer, the DSP, was given a notice. The students were probably telling him about their demand, and the notice asked the British government to quit India or face the consequences.
3. Babu and Manju were a bit disappointed with the way the students were marching. What was the reason?
They expected a noisy protest, with slogans, dance or a drama, but the students marched quietly, without any shouts.
4. What had the police expected about the way of protest? How did the student leaders manage the protest?

The police expected the students to protest and be violent, so that they could beat them up and take them to jail. The leaders avoided violence by marching silently, handing over a notice, shouting ‘Mahatma Gandhi Ki Jai’ and marching back peacefully.
5. What was there in the ‘mysterious parcel’? What suspicion did the police have about that?
The parcel contained a cyclostyling machine. The police suspected that the family was making copies of Mahatma Gandhi’s speech and hiding people in the house.
6. Why had Patil, the sub-inspector, come there? Who believed him? What was the result?

He came to warn them that a search would be carried out that night, as he was a friend of Amma’s late husband from school. Amma believed him and handed over the machine, so that Suman and the material were saved. Patil took the machine away and then left with Mohan and Suman.
7. What do you think the writer of the incident is trying to impress upon the readers?

lessons.notes: Dicky Dolma climbed Mt. Everest on 10 May 1993, aged 19, becoming the youngest woman to do so.
ab: I. Answer the following questions briefly
1. Give an account of Dicky Dolma’s hardships and challenges before she was qualified for scaling the peak.

She lost her mother at the age of 11 and later her elder brother. Her family faced financial hardship because her father was bedridden and needed money for his treatment. She had to overcome her own worries and difficulties in training, while also having the strength to keep going.
2. How has Dolma described her preparedness for the task of scaling Mount Everest?

She had been fascinated by the Himalayan peaks since childhood and trained at the mountaineering institute in Manali, where she scored ‘A’ grades. She was selected after three successful expeditions, practised for four hours daily and was not afraid of hard work.
II. Answer the following questions
1. ‘With zeal and determination there is nothing that one cannot achieve.’ What else do you think is necessary to achieve, besides zeal and determination?

2. Narrate the adventurous story of Dicky Dolma in your own words.

ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Sample: Dicky Dolma, born in Palchan, Himachal Pradesh, lost her mother and brother early in life. Fascinated by the snow-clad Himalayas, she took up mountaineering at Manali and was selected for the Everest expedition. On 10 May 1993, at the age of 19, she reached the summit and became the youngest woman to climb Everest. Despite her father’s illness and financial problems, she remained determined and later began teaching mountaineering.
